findings.explanation: high confidence. A direct system (or filtered diagram) requires that the indexing poset/category is directed (as defined in Definition 2.8: every finite subset has an upper bound). A spanning tree $T'$ of an arbitrary connected graph is not directed unless it is a linear chain; in general, an oriented tree contains vertices with no common upper bound, and any tree with branches cannot have common upper bounds without creating undirected cycles. Consequently, the diagram indexed by $T'$ is not a directed system. As a result, the colimit $\varinjlim F_i$ over $T'$ is not a filtered colimit, which causes the subsequent arguments to fail: canonical maps $F_i \to F$ need not be monomorphisms, maps from finitely generated modules into the colimit do not factor through some single $F_i$ (as was asserted in the proof of Lemma 3.6), and the colimit does not commute with finite limits or preserve the stated properties. Witness: Consider three f-simples with V_1 -> V_2 <- V_3. The underlying graph of this diagram is a tree, but it is not a directed set (there are no morphisms out of V_2). If instead we have V_1 <- V_0 -> V_2, there is no upper bound for {V_1, V_2} in the tree, so it is not directed. Adding a common upper bound in a graph with multiple branches creates cycles, violating the definition of a tree.

evidence.text: This gives a directed system of $f$−simples consisting of monomorphisms (we don't have any compatibility condition to check on the maps as the underlying graph is a tree), therefore we can use Lemma 3.6
